items.title: Show HN: Run AI-generated logic safely inside your app
items.summary: Stof is an open-source runtime for logic you don't own or fully trust. Imagine a JSON document with functions inside, scoped to just the document that contains them. Stof instantiates this doc as a small wasm env, and makes these functions safe to call. They can't access or manipulate anything but their own doc. WebAssembly by itself is large in binary form, requires a lot of tooling, etc. Stof can be sent over the wire easily, is a superset of JSON for compatibility, and keeps the guarantees. I created Stof not to replace a data format or anything, but to be a glue layer for data and distributed systems to work with one another. This includes I/O for interchange data like JSON, YAML, TOML, etc., but also complex data like PDFs, images, binaries, both structured and unstructured (good layer to turn one into the other). The fact is, the layer of data and communication between apps tends to be a bit messy, and strict adapters compiled at build time tend to be insufficient for the dynamism of modern software. This applies directly to AI-generated data and code, which is basically like calling into another untrusted service. With this, you can safely embed the execution, pick where things run, and combine harnesses like data. Works well as a "living" context, also with the JSON interop - just parse into or stringify sections of the Stof doc at runtime when needed, like agent tool defs. The playground on the site runs entirely in your browser. Stof is written in Rust and has support for JS/TS and Python today. I'd especially like feedback on whether the idea makes sense from the landing page, and where the docs need help. GitHub: https://github.com/dev-formata-io/stof Thank you!! -CJ

items.title: Page One Open Source Screenwriting App
Show HN: Petal, open-source CoScreen/ScreenHero finally free
items.summary: Hi HN! I’m Jason Thomas, one of the founders of CoScreen. As some of you may know, Datadog sunset the CoScreen service on July 31st. Four of us from the original CoScreen team have spent the last couple months building a free and open source pair programming tool inspired by those that came before us: It’s called Petal ( https://github.com/kiruna-labs/petal ) Some history first, because when we started CoScreen we had hoped to break the sad and established pattern of this industry. Screenhero was an exceptional tool that a lot of us loved for pairing. Multiple cursors, low latency, you could click your partner’s editor, and just start typing. It felt like magic while we had it. Then Slack bought it in 2015, and shut down the standalone app in December 2017. When Till, Max, and I started CoScreen, we were aware of this history, and wanted to build an even more magical collaboration and screen sharing experience: the entire concept was “throw a window from your laptop up on someone else’s screen, and start collaborating with zero friction.” Datadog acquired us in 2022, and thus began the great adventure of adapting our real-time technology into Datadog products, while also continue developing CoScreen as a standalone tool from the Datadog ecosystem. Datadog invested in the product for years and we’re thankful for that. But CoScreen itself proved, like so many other screen sharing tool acquisitions, to be too tangential from the customer base and core mission. We instead built other communication features in Datadog, the integrations with other video platforms, and also its wildly successful MCP server. We weren't the only ones. Around was bought by Miro and shut down in March 2025. Multi (formerly Remotion) was acqui-hired by OpenAI in 2024 and shut down about a month later. It's nearly always the same story: a small team builds something hard that people love, a platform buys it for the team or the feature, and the standalone product doesn't survive the integration. So we decided firmly to do things differently this time. Petal is completely free and open source and we aren't monetizing it. If we lose interest or get hit by a bus, you can self-host it or fork it, and nobody can sunset it on you. Honestly it's a love letter to everyone in this community that supported us, believed in us, and to liberate collaborative screen sharing from this vicious cycle. We hope through this we can help foster a large and vibrant community around innovating in this product sector. What Petal does: shared windows show up as real windows on your desktop, movable and resizable, not tiles in a grid. Several people can share at once, everyone gets a labeled cursor, and you can click into any shared window to type and scroll. Rooms are persistent, so you click once to join "eng-sync" instead of passing links around. It runs on macOS and Windows (Linux is next, this time for real and you can help us!), plus a web app. Media goes over LiveKit. You can use our hosted instance with zero config, or point the app at your own LiveKit server with one docker-compose if you want the traffic to stay on your network or even use an entirely different video backend if you want to. The part that still feels strange to us: CoScreen took almost six years to build. The first version of Petal took under eight weeks, from scratch, with frontier models like Fable and Astra doing a lot of the work. Real-time video and window capture is some of the most unforgiving code we have ever written, so we didn't expect that. We will do a proper writeup on what worked and what didn't, and are happy to answer questions about it here. Till, Darren, Max and I will be in the thread.

Show HN: OWASP Finbot Defended with Tenuo
items.summary: Tenuo is a task-scoped authz primitive for agentic work. We are an open protocol and an open source implementation at github.com/tenuo-ai/tenuo We created a fork of OWASP finbot with Tenuo wired in and red-teamed it with promptfoo. We went from 50 successful attacks to 0 with Tenuo. The promptfoo attacks were able to fool the model, but the deterministic guardrails Tenuo provides stopped it from acting on the poisoned instructions.

items.title: Show HN: Turn newsletters and blogs into a podcast feed
items.summary: Newsletter to Podcast is an open-source Python tool that turns newsletters and blogs into an RSS podcast feed! You can pick the sources, generate audio, and subscribe to the resulting feed in a podcast app that supports custom RSS (I use Castbox). The project supports full article narration as well as spoken summaries. Full narration uses Edge TTS and needs no API key; summaries use Gemini and require your own key (though the free limit is quite generous)! You can set a maximum episode length and longer full readings split into numbered parts at natural text boundaries. There’s a prerecorded sample on the demo page, and a simple command in the README that fetches an original sample article and generates fresh audio without an API key. The package can run locally or on a schedule in your own GitHub repository using GitHub Actions! I wanted to turn some of my favorite newsletters into podcasts (like Seth’s Blog and A Learning A Day) and couldn’t find a free and simple solution that already existed. Let me know what you think! Demo: https://akspad.github.io/newsletter-to-podcast/

items.title: Show HN: CueLight – open-source <2mb/0.5M param always listening turn detector
items.summary: Before I get into the details, I'd just like to say I was able to build this thanks to the work done by the people who work on Pipecat & SmartTurn as this relied on their data. SmartTurn is a fantastic open source model for turn detection. I needed a much smaller version that could fit anywhere and be always on (always actually being every 20ms in this case), so I figured I could do a trade off of making it support one language only (English), not rely on building on top of a Whisper model and possibly squeeze out similar performance. While I do still wish to improve this model significantly, this is my progress in doing so thus far. I also augmented the data with synthetic noise and reverb to try to improve its scores in handling those situations. I'd love for people to try it, and even better, provide suggestions or audio that can help me improve it. The link takes you to a sample of it running in the browser. There's also an SSM version but that was purely for experimental purposes. While SSMs do well on streaming, there isn't much to gain from it here, since long memory of audio stream isn't that important for turn detection, just the most recent few seconds really, so the GRU version does just fine (or better) and uses much less CPU. More details are in the repo: https://github.com/sshah03/CueLight For those interested in SmartTurn: https://github.com/pipecat-ai/smart-turn
